summary: McLatchie wins narrowly by offering the more developed comparative explanation, while Paulogia exposes serious unresolved dependence on Gospel proximity, transmission, and source-specific reliability.

pro.text: the best or most probable explanation is that Jesus rose from the dead
pro.context: McLatchie states his actual comparative conclusion in the final summary after distinguishing probability from logical necessity.

con.text: I think a naturalistic explanation is the best option
con.context: Paulogia closes by moving beyond mere possibility and explicitly endorsing a naturalistic explanation as comparatively preferable.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie reframed his obligation as explanation: resurrection need only outperform live alternatives, not become deductively unavoidable, and this corrected Paulogia’s repeated use of required. Principal limitation: The clarification came after the opening burden had already drifted, however, and McLatchie still needed to specify a common measure by which textual reliability, sincere error, fabrication, and resurrection could be compared. Live burden: His remaining task was therefore to show that the maximal Gospel data deserved enough confidence and discriminative force to make natural competitors less probable, while avoiding any inference from mere survival or unexplained detail. Locked score: 92/100 — Because he identified the proper motion-level standard clearly and used it consistently thereafter, yet left important probability assignments implicit, this strategically decisive correction earns 92 rather than a perfect score.
moves.words: McLatchie defines the proposition as comparative probability rather than deductive necessity. after Paulogia repeatedly framed resurrection as a required or uniquely possible origin.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia observed that Christian commitment cannot distinguish an accurate resurrection belief from a sincere but mistaken one, since either belief can motivate sacrifice, evangelism, and institutional persistence across centuries. Principal limitation: That point sharply limits appeals to Christianity’s subsequent cultural success, but it says much less about earliest named proclaimers whose access, experiences, and risks were the contested evidence. Live burden: He still had to connect motivational equivalence to a historically grounded origin scenario and demonstrate that an initial sincere error could generate the encounter traditions without relying only on abstract possibility. Locked score: 84/100 — The argument efficiently blocked an overinference from endurance to truth, while its reach stopped short of the earliest links, so the locked score of 84 reflects strong relevance with incomplete explanatory development.
moves.words: Paulogia argues that true and mistaken resurrection beliefs can motivate identical commitment. while limiting what later Christian endurance can establish about the initiating event.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie presented a lucid organizing trilemma—truth, honest mistake, or deceit—and tied mistake to multisensory group encounters and deceit to costly proclamation, giving his opening a coherent route from source reliability to resurrection. Principal limitation: Its apparent exhaustiveness depended on treating Gospel encounter reports as substantially unembellished eyewitness testimony, precisely the premise Paulogia disputed through oral development and literary dependence. Live burden: The case therefore still needed independent support for proximity and transmission before the encounter detail or persecution evidence could do the exclusionary work assigned to it, and mixed or gradually developing explanations required attention. Locked score: 79/100 — Because the framework was and responsive to the motion but front-loaded its most controversial premise, 79 appropriately rewards structure and explanatory ambition while withholding credit for an established conclusion.
moves.words: McLatchie organizes the case around resurrection, honest mistake, or deliberate deceit. with source reliability functioning as the necessary gateway to both exclusions.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s opening mapped a accuracy-and-sincerity spectrum and emphasized that Christianity could begin through sincere mistake, embellishment, or fabrication without a physical resurrection, exposing weakness of any necessity claim. Principal limitation: Yet the motion asked which explanation is best, and his early demand that every nonresurrection point be impossible substituted possibility for comparative probability until his closing statement finally endorsed naturalistic preference. Live burden: He consequently retained the burden to identify a concrete natural pathway, connect it to the surviving evidence, and compare its explanatory costs against McLatchie’s cumulative case rather than keeping alternatives open. Locked score: 70/100 — The opening deserves 70 because it created underdetermination and framed rival classes, but its initial burden standard was misaligned with the proposition and delayed the positive comparison Paulogia ultimately needed.
moves.words: Paulogia opens a spectrum of natural origins but initially emphasizes possibility over probability. before his closing finally asserted a positive preference for natural explanation.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia plausibly stressed that many combinations of sincerity and accuracy could produce an originating proclamation, preventing McLatchie from treating resurrection as the only conceivable route to Christianity’s existence. Principal limitation: His spectrum, however, grouped different mechanisms together and did not explain which person was mistaken, what experience occurred, how the belief became bodily resurrection testimony, or why narratives acquired their specific shape. Live burden: The unresolved burden was to move from a large possibility space to one evidentially supported competitor whose probability and explanatory scope could be weighed against the maximal-data resurrection account. Locked score: 63/100 — Since this move successfully denied logical entailment but offered little discrimination among its own alternatives, the score of 63 records a defensive contribution that remained too indeterminate to establish naturalistic superiority.
moves.words: Paulogia maintains that numerous sincere or deceptive natural pathways remain compatible with Christianity. without selecting and developing one natural competitor through the surviving historical evidence.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s closing met wording of the motion by stating that a naturalistic explanation was the best option and tied that preference to Gospel dependence, elaboration, and failures of transfer from mundane accuracy to supernatural claims. Principal limitation: The conclusion remained broader than its support, because thousands of possible explanations do not collectively raise the probability of any account, and his favored single-mistake story was sparsely specified. Live burden: He needed to show how the initiating error survived transmission into multiple bodily encounter narratives and why that developmental pathway was more probable than McLatchie’s account after granting interconnections. Locked score: 78/100 — The score of 78 recognizes a relevant position and a warning about cross-domain transfer, while reflecting that the comparative naturalistic model arrived late and never received construction.
moves.words: Paulogia finally states that a naturalistic explanation best fits the available evidence. while retaining the single-mistake hypothesis and rejecting transfer from mundane textual accuracy.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie’s foot-washing example produced a concrete interlocking detail: Luke supplies dispute over greatness that naturally explains Jesus washing the disciples’ feet in John, although neither writer overtly constructs the connection. Principal limitation: This is evidence of remembered circumstances or shared material, but the same fit can arise through tradition, source knowledge, or narrative development and does not by itself identify eyewitness authorship. Live burden: He had to establish independence and casualness across enough examples, then explain why reliability in ministry episodes should increase confidence in resurrection appearances rather than only in a historical kernel. Locked score: 79/100 — The move earns 79 because its textual observation is and probative against pure invention, while alternative transmission routes and the later supernatural inference limit how much weight it can carry.
moves.words: McLatchie uses the foot-washing and greatness dispute as an incidental textual interlock. offered as evidence that separate Gospel details preserve connected historical circumstances.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia offered a recognizable transmission mechanism in which persuasive details survive, objections invite elaboration, Mark records traditions, and Matthew, Luke, and John reshape earlier material, challenging an eyewitness interpretation of interconnections. Principal limitation: The model fits literary dependence generally, yet in this debate it was mostly asserted and illustrated through analogy rather than shown to generate McLatchie’s subtler examples without deliberate coordination. Live burden: His remaining burden was to distinguish oral selection from post hoc accommodation, date additions, and show how development explains both casual cross-account fits and the resurrection narratives without assuming every useful detail was selected. Locked score: 75/100 — At 75, the move supplies a competing process and exposes underdetermination, but its causal particulars remain less demonstrated than the confidence of Paulogia’s evolutionary description suggests.
moves.words: Paulogia proposes oral selection, embellishment, and literary dependence as a natural transmission process. to explain persuasive detail without granting eyewitness authorship or independent resurrection testimony.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie improved the undesigned-coincidence argument by focusing on casual, artless details such as the Passover chronology across Mark and John, arguing that readers commonly miss the fit and that neither account appears written to explain the other. Principal limitation: This criterion gives a principled reason to distinguish interlock from obvious harmonization, although subtlety alone cannot exclude common tradition, indirect dependence, editorial compression, or coincidences discovered through selective comparison. Live burden: He needed a broader controlled set showing that such fits occur more specifically under independent access than under literary development, and he had to connect chronology to resurrection testimony. Locked score: 83/100 — The locked 83 reflects a sophisticated discriminator with value, tempered by unresolved base-rate and selection concerns and by the limited transfer from mundane narrative detail.
moves.words: McLatchie argues that subtle, artless chronological fits distinguish memory from designed harmonization. through Passover chronology that neither Mark nor John overtly explains for readers.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia correctly located the decisive hinge in McLatchie’s maximal-data reply: multisensory encounters exclude mistake if Gospel authors or their sources reliably preserve what purported eyewitnesses actually reported. Principal limitation: His challenge prevented the vividness of narratives from silently becoming evidence about the originating experiences, and it coherently joined his oral-development account to the honest-mistake alternative. Live burden: Nevertheless, denying a demonstrated eyewitness connection was not itself evidence for a specific developmental history; he still needed to engage McLatchie’s authorship, Acts, Pauline, and interconnection arguments rather than treating uncertainty as positive support. Locked score: 87/100 — The score of 87 rewards this precise exposure of premise dependence and its effect on the trilemma, while recognizing that Paulogia weakened McLatchie’s inference more successfully than he established his own transmission model.
moves.words: Paulogia challenges whether Gospel writers or sources were genuinely connected to eyewitnesses. making vivid encounter detail conditional on a source connection that remained contested.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie candidly granted a strong candidate discrepancy between Mark and John and analyzed its two epistemic directions: contradiction reduces reliability, while divergent presentation can support independence and thereby strengthen some interconnections. Principal limitation: This avoided simplistic harmonization and showed that features may cut differently, but independence inferred from disagreement does not guarantee truth, nor does every discrepancy license credit for independent attestation. Live burden: He had to estimate whether positive independence signal outweighed negative accuracy cost in the passages and demonstrate that the sources were independent specifically where resurrection evidence mattered. Locked score: 88/100 — The move merits 88 because it was unusually balanced, responsive, and methodologically mature, with the remaining deduction reflecting the absence of a calibrated net assessment rather than any failure to acknowledge contrary evidence.
moves.words: McLatchie grants discrepancies can reduce reliability while also supporting source independence. rather than treating contradiction as either wholly destructive or automatically independence-confirming.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s Star Wars comparison effectively demonstrated logical point that independently presented details can interlock within an invented or developed narrative world, so an apparent undesigned coincidence does not entail truth. Principal limitation: The analogy captured how audience questions and successive retellings might supply explanatory details, but a deliberately coordinated multimedia franchise differs materially from ancient oral transmission and cannot establish equal probabilities. Live burden: He needed historical evidence that the Gospel tradition underwent the proposed objection-driven elaboration and a criterion explaining when casualness ceases to favor independent memory over adaptive storytelling. Locked score: 83/100 — The score of 83 reflects a memorable and analytically defeater to overclaiming, balanced against the analogy’s limited historical fit and its inability by itself to explain the distribution of Gospel agreements and differences.
moves.words: Paulogia uses fictional narrative interlocks to show coherence does not entail historical truth. through a Star Wars analogy involving separately presented but mutually explanatory narrative details.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie explained inferential bridge: numerous confirmations would support the Gospel writers as informed and truthful, which would then justify using their detailed resurrection encounters to evaluate honest mistake and using persecution to evaluate deceit. Principal limitation: This is more than claiming that one accurate detail proves every supernatural report, yet the bridge remains probabilistic and vulnerable to compartmental accuracy, theological elaboration, and unequal source quality across episodes. Live burden: He needed to quantify or compare how mundane confirmations raise confidence in the appearance material, while independently securing the persecution premise and avoiding circular reliance on Acts. Locked score: 84/100 — The locked 84 rewards a coherent architecture that answers the relevance question, but preserves a substantial deduction because the contested transfer is the very step Paulogia never granted.
moves.words: McLatchie says ordinary confirmations justify applying encounter detail and sincerity evidence cumulatively. so ordinary reliability can support later evaluation of mistake and deliberate deception.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia made a distinction between granting true ministry kernels and accepting resurrection narratives, noting that accuracy in one portion of a document does not automatically validate another, especially when accounts of appearances do not straightforwardly corroborate. Principal limitation: This checked McLatchie’s attempt to let mundane interconnections underwrite trilemma and preserved appropriate claim-by-claim scrutiny rather than an all-true or all-false treatment of sources. Live burden: His burden remained to assess whether authorial reliability nevertheless changes resurrection reports’ probability and to defend his assertion that the appearances elaborate First Corinthians rather than represent partly independent testimony. Locked score: 89/100 — With a score of 89, this is among Paulogia’s strongest moves because it isolates an invalid automatic transfer, though it does not show that every calibrated reliability transfer is negligible.
moves.words: Paulogia denies that accurate ministry details automatically authenticate supernatural resurrection reports. especially when appearance narratives do not straightforwardly corroborate the same reported event.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie argued that public group appearances, conversations, touch, eating, and repeated events across forty days would be extraordinarily difficult for the witnesses to misperceive, giving the honest-mistake horn concrete evidential pressure. Principal limitation: The force of this argument is conditional on the later Gospel descriptions preserving early testimony; without that premise, narrative detail measures the final texts rather than the originating experience that Paulogia hypothesized. Live burden: He therefore still had to establish source proximity and independence strongly enough to block hallucination, misidentification, visionary interpretation, and gradual embellishment at the correct historical stage. Locked score: 80/100 — The score of 80 reflects substantial explanatory power once the reports are admitted and a answer to vague mistake proposals, discounted because the crucial authenticity condition remained disputed throughout the debate.
moves.words: McLatchie argues repeated multisensory group encounters are difficult to explain by honest mistake. provided those Gospel descriptions substantially preserve what the earliest witnesses actually claimed.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia identified a parsimonious candidate in which one sincere but mistaken individual, possibly Peter, initiates resurrection belief, thereby showing why later willingness to suffer need not imply that original interpretation was accurate. Principal limitation: The proposal remained a sketch: it did not specify the precipitating experience, the transition to a bodily claim, the role of Paul and other named witnesses, or the growth of multiple detailed encounter traditions. Live burden: To become a explanation, it needed independent support and a transmission account demonstrating that one error predicts the texts better than resurrection or several partially independent experiences. Locked score: 69/100 — The score of 69 credits its focused challenge to the deceit-versus-truth framing, while marking the large gap between a logically possible origin and a developed, evidence-sensitive rival.
moves.words: Paulogia proposes one sincerely mistaken originator as a sufficient natural starting point. but leaves the initiating experience and subsequent bodily elaboration largely unspecified.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie answered sincere-origin challenge by conceding that minimal facts underdetermine experience types and then arguing that maximal Gospel data provide multisensory, conversational, repeated encounters needed to resist honest mistake. Principal limitation: This was a serious qualification rather than an evasion, and it accurately exposed why First Corinthians alone cannot carry his conclusion, but it increased dependence on contested Gospel authorship and transmission reliability. Live burden: His remaining burden was to prove that these richly detailed reports are early, independent, and unembellished enough to describe the witnesses rather than narrative development. Locked score: 86/100 — The move earns 86 for diagnosing the minimal-facts weakness and offering a stronger conditional response, with the deduction reflecting that its superior discriminatory power arrives after acceptance of the debate’s most disputed source premise.
moves.words: McLatchie rejects minimal facts and relies on richer Gospel encounter descriptions. because First Corinthians alone leaves too many different experience types compatible with resurrection belief.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie used voluntary hardships, imprisonments, dangers, and changed conduct to argue that early proclaimers sincerely believed their resurrection testimony, appropriately directing the evidence against deliberate deception rather than treating suffering as proof of truth. Principal limitation: The initial formulation spoke broadly of apostles and leaned on Paley, leaving uncertain which witnesses made which claims, what costs they knowingly accepted, and how securely those links are documented. Live burden: He still needed named, source-specific chains connecting an alleged eyewitness to a resurrection assertion and voluntary persistence under avoidable pressure, while separating later Christian persecution from first-generation evidence. Locked score: 76/100 — The score of 76 recognizes the valid sincerity principle and relevance, but reflects that categories of costly proclamation did not yet meet Paulogia’s demand for historically discriminating particulars.
moves.words: McLatchie argues voluntary hardship makes deliberate apostolic deception considerably less plausible. although the opening formulation did not yet provide witness-by-witness historical links.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia’s demand for names, precise resurrection claims, evidence of preaching, and records of voluntary risk exposed how easily generic references to apostles can conceal missing links between experience, proclamation, and suffering. Principal limitation: This challenge narrowed martyrdom discussion and forced McLatchie to concede limited evidence for deaths and the uncertain availability of recantation under Nero. Live burden: Paulogia still had to reckon with evidence of nonfatal hardship and imprisonment, since sincerity can be supported without a formal execution choice, and his questioning did not establish that all links were absent. Locked score: 90/100 — The score of 90 reflects excellent burden control and source sensitivity that materially improved the debate, with a modest deduction because the critique sometimes treated insufficiently evidence as though it carried almost no weight.
moves.words: Paulogia demands named witnesses, precise claims, documented preaching, and voluntary risk. before allowing broad claims about apostles to count as evidence of sincerity.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie refined his claim by declining the common martyrdom argument, limiting named deaths, acknowledging Nero’s political motives and probable lack of recantation opportunities, and instead appealing to a broader context of voluntarily endured danger and imprisonment. Principal limitation: This modest formulation accurately targets sincerity and avoids claiming that suffering proves resurrection, but much of its historical support still depends on Acts being substantially trustworthy and on identifying the relevant sufferers as witnesses. Live burden: He needed to secure those connections without circularly using the same source whose reliability was contested and to distinguish voluntary exposure for testimony from generalized hostility toward Christians. Locked score: 85/100 — The score of 85 rewards unusually concessions and a defensible evidential claim, while retaining deductions for source dependence and incomplete person-by-person linkage.
moves.words: McLatchie narrows persecution evidence to general hardship supporting sincerity rather than truth. after conceding limited martyrdom evidence, political motives, and uncertain opportunities to recant.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia correctly emphasized that persecution can establish sincerity while leaving sincere mistake untouched, and his question whether even five people could be mistaken prevented debate from sliding from honest commitment to factual accuracy. Principal limitation: This response precisely limited probative target of McLatchie’s evidence and preserved the distinction between the deceit and mistake horns of the trilemma. Live burden: However, he still needed to confront whether several independent, detailed, repeated experiences would make collective mistake unlikely; simply asking whether mistake is possible did not answer the maximal-data comparison. Locked score: 91/100 — The score of 91 reflects a decisive logical limitation on persecution evidence and faithful burden tracking, with the remaining deduction arising because the proposed alternative remained underdescribed once multiple witnesses and encounter contents were conditionally granted.
moves.words: Paulogia stresses that sincere suffering cannot distinguish accurate belief from honest error. even if several named proclaimers voluntarily accepted danger for their resurrection belief.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie argued that miracles must deviate from nature to function as divine signs and that wider Christian evidence—Paul’s conversion, prophecy, Jesus’ identity claims, contemporary miracles, and Israel—could raise prior probability of resurrection. Principal limitation: This supplied a coherent Bayesian response to automatic dismissal, but most supporting categories were mentioned rather than defended within the debate and risked expanding the case far beyond the shared record. Live burden: He still had to show that these independent considerations genuinely favor Christian divine action without presupposing disputed theology, and then combine that prior with the reliability of the specific resurrection testimony. Locked score: 75/100 — The score of 75 recognizes a philosophically framework and religious-context explanation, while heavily discounting unsupported auxiliary claims that could not bear their assigned prior-shifting role here.
moves.words: McLatchie uses divine-sign context and wider Christian evidence to raise miracle priors. rather than allowing deviation from nature itself to disqualify resurrection from consideration.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia highlighted the frequent reality of error and deception against the rarity of miracles, explaining why testimonial failure initially appears more probable than resurrection and why Gospel testimony faces a demanding threshold. Principal limitation: This is a legitimate prior-probability concern, but his first formulation approached an absolute ceiling on testimony and compared raw daily frequencies without accounting for evidence quality, independence, specificity, or divine-context hypotheses. Live burden: He needed a calibrated account of how the prior should update under different testimonial conditions and a direct assessment of the actual sources rather than a categorical appeal to methodological naturalism. Locked score: 76/100 — The score of 76 credits the central probabilistic challenge and its relevance to best explanation, while reflecting overstatement that McLatchie could correctly identify as mathematically untenable.
moves.words: Paulogia argues common error and deception outweigh rare miracles absent extraordinary testimony. while initially approaching an unjustified ceiling on what sufficiently strong testimony could establish.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: McLatchie replied that if testimony provides any likelihood advantage for a proposition, sufficient quantity and quality can in principle overcome a low prior, exposing mathematical problem with an absolute testimonial barrier. Principal limitation: The response established a general updating rule but did not show that these Gospel reports possess the required independence, reliability, and likelihood ratio, which remained the substantive dispute. Live burden: He had to translate his source arguments into a comparative case strong enough to cross Paulogia’s admitted high threshold and account for dependence among accounts. Locked score: 91/100 — The score of 91 rewards a concise, rigorous correction with philosophical force, while stopping short of full credit because proving that testimony can overcome a prior is not demonstrating that these disputed ancient accounts actually do.
moves.words: McLatchie replies that sufficiently strong testimony can mathematically overcome a low prior. without yet demonstrating that these dependent ancient accounts meet that evidential threshold.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Paulogia qualified his position by admitting uncertainty about whether any amount of testimony could suffice, suggesting that one hundred independent cases might establish that something happened, and returning attention to dependence among Gospels. Principal limitation: This retreat avoided a strict impossibility claim and revealed the disagreement as threshold and source independence rather than a simple ban on miracles. Live burden: Yet methodological naturalism remained only loosely connected to a numerical or standard, and he did not explain what evidence would identify the correct cause after the threshold was crossed or why the existing accounts fall so far below it. Locked score: 86/100 — The score of 86 reflects intellectual candor and an dependence objection, moderated by an underdeveloped updating rule and a residual reluctance to specify falsifiable conditions.
moves.words: Paulogia qualifies his threshold while maintaining that Gospel dependence prevents sufficient cumulative force. by allowing hypothetical independent cases to matter while denying comparable independence here.

strengths: McLatchie corrected the central burden from deductive necessity to comparative probability and kept his later case focused on the best-explanation question.
He integrated source interconnections, detailed encounters, and costly proclamation into a cumulative trilemma rather than treating any single consideration as decisive.
He made unusually careful concessions about discrepancies, minimal-facts underdetermination, martyrdom evidence, Nero’s motives, and the limited role of persecution.

blunders.text: His case depended heavily on the contested transfer from mundane textual reliability to the authenticity of detailed resurrection narratives without sufficiently calibrating that transfer.
Several claims offered to raise the miracle prior—prophecy, contemporary miracles, Israel, and Jesus’ identity claims—were introduced without enough debate-specific defense.

strengths: Paulogia repeatedly separated sincerity from truth and showed why persecution cannot resolve the live possibility of honest mistake.
He exposed the dependence of the maximal-data case on eyewitness proximity and rejected any automatic move from accurate historical kernels to supernatural accuracy.
His demands for named witnesses, precise claims, documented risks, and source independence forced useful narrowing and concessions from McLatchie.

blunders.text: His opening often treated the survival of any natural possibility as sufficient, even though the motion required a comparative case for the best explanation.
The favored single-sincere-origin hypothesis remained underdescribed and lacked a detailed path from an initiating error to multiple bodily encounter traditions.

finalArgument.thesis: The resurrection becomes the best explanation only if independently supported source reliability makes the detailed encounter reports substantially more expected than oral development would.
premises: Casual interconnections and resistant discrepancies can jointly support partial independence when their distribution is less likely under deliberate harmonization or direct literary copying.
Partial independence raises confidence in encounter detail only when the same source relationships hold in the resurrection passages rather than merely in ordinary ministry narratives.
If repeated group conversations, touch, eating, and extended appearances preserve early testimony, a single sincere misidentification predicts the reported data poorly.
Voluntarily endured danger then updates sincerity rather than truth, narrowing deliberate fabrication without independently excluding error or establishing supernatural causation.
A religious-context prior can matter only insofar as its supporting evidence is defended independently of the resurrection conclusion being assessed.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the cumulative resurrection case succeeds comparatively when source-specific independence and preservation are established strongly enough that detailed honest mistake and coordinated development become less probable together.

newArguments.title: Distributional Independence Test
newArguments.text: Instead of treating every interconnection as equal, compare where subtle fits and genuine discrepancies occur across the documents. Independent memory predicts uneven agreement, incidental chronology, and unforced explanatory links alongside mistakes; direct copying predicts closer verbal or structural dependence; later harmonization predicts conspicuous repairs. Applying those rival predictions specifically to resurrection passages would determine whether mundane interconnections legitimately raise confidence in encounter content.

newArguments.title: Sequential Horn Updating
newArguments.text: The trilemma should be evaluated as a sequence of conditional updates rather than three labels. First estimate whether the reports preserve early witness claims; then ask what those reported experiences imply about mistake; only afterward use voluntary hardship to update deception. This prevents source confidence, encounter detail, and sincerity from being counted repeatedly while showing exactly which evidential link must carry each part of the resurrection inference.

finalArgument.thesis: A naturalistic explanation becomes preferable only when a specified developmental pathway predicts the textual evidence better than authenticated, independent reports of bodily encounters do.
premises: Accurate mundane details can survive oral transmission or literary reuse without guaranteeing that later supernatural episodes preserve equally reliable testimony.
A sincere initiating experience can motivate proclamation and sacrifice even when its interpretation is false, so persecution discriminates deception from sincerity but not mistake from resurrection.
Narrative dependence, increasing physical detail, and objection-responsive elaboration would be expected if a sparse originating claim developed during repeated transmission.
The single-origin hypothesis must nevertheless explain Paul, named appearance traditions, group claims, and variations among accounts rather than relying on their bare logical compatibility.
Low miracle priors create a demanding threshold, but testimony must remain capable in principle of crossing it when independence, specificity, and reliability become sufficiently strong.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore the naturalistic case wins only if a historically anchored sincere-error model explains both early proclamation and later bodily detail with fewer unsupported assumptions than McLatchie’s contested source-authentication pathway.

newArguments.title: Transmission Gradient Prediction
newArguments.text: A developed sincere-error model predicts a traceable gradient from earlier sparse formulations to later concrete scenes, with additions clustering around apologetic pressures such as mistaken identity, physicality, and group verification. Testing that pattern across First Corinthians and the Gospel strata would give Paulogia a positive explanatory measure. A stable early distribution of the same difficult details across independent sources would count strongly against the model.

newArguments.title: Witness Link Matrix
newArguments.text: Construct a separate chain for every proposed witness: claimed experience, earliest attestation, access of the reporting source, public proclamation, documented hardship, and opportunity to avoid that hardship. Empty links would prevent generic references to apostles from accumulating unwarranted force, while completed links would constrain the single-origin theory. This method converts the persecution disagreement into auditable evidence and preserves the crucial distinction between sincerity and accuracy.

editorialReview.sourceFidelity: I checked every summary, description, critique, and extension against the direct debate material while excluding audience questions, logistics, promotions, and corrupted transcript clauses.
editorialReview.completeQuotes: I verified that both featured quotations reproduce complete eligible thoughts exactly: McLatchie’s comparative resurrection conclusion and Paulogia’s naturalistic preference.
editorialReview.scoreConsistency: I confirmed the 83–80 overall result and preserved every one of the twenty-five locked move scores without recalculation, substitution, or drift.
editorialReview.nonformulaicCritiques: I reviewed paired critiques together and ensured each explains a move-specific strength, limitation, unresolved burden, and score rationale from its actual exchange.
editorialReview.aiContributionNonformulaic: I checked that the four AI extensions add distinct testable reasoning through distribution, sequential updating, transmission gradients, and witness-link analysis.
editorialReview.aiPunctuation: I reviewed the AI prose for natural sentence structure and punctuation, avoiding mirrored scaffolds, fragments, canned transitions, and mechanical sentence-bank construction.
editorialReview.referenceComparison: I compared the final evaluation with the supplied reference metrics only for calibration and did not import claims, scores, or language from another debate.
